trivial_interview_questions.question: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: The thing that I look to achieve in the short term, i.e. 5 years, is mastering the core responsibilities of this role and positioning myself as a reliable technical expert within the team. At this point, I would want to start taking responsibility for complex end-to-end projects and mentoring less experienced developers. Ideally, I see myself evolving into a leadership position where I can influence the technical strategy to contribute to the organization's strategic objectives.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Why should we hire you over other candidates?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: What differentiates me from other candidates is my technical competence and bias for execution. I am always looking at how I can solve a technical problem with a higher business impact, not just one-off issues. Throughout the years, I have demonstrated my ability to be quick in technical learning and bring a cross-functional perspective to execution. I can bring high accountability, eagerness to raise the bar, and focus on the project delivery to make a positive contribution.

trivial_interview_questions.question: What is your biggest weakness?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: In my earlier career, I used to jump into code implementation before doing proper documentation or architectural considerations to justify my technical decisions to the team. I learned that to be a good engineer, I need to invest time in my documentation and spec reviews. Now I consciously use that time to do a preliminary write-up or even run an RFC before writing core logic that will help the other engineers to easily understand my code.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed or made a mistake.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: There was this one time when I deployed a module update that introduced a performance bottleneck due to a particular load condition that I did not consider during the pre-production testing. As soon as the issue was flagged by the telemetry dashboard, I alerted the team, rolled back the deployment, and shared the resolution steps with the stakeholders. In the subsequent days, I did a thorough analysis and enhanced our CI/CD platform with performance tests to prevent similar occurrences.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you handle tight deadlines or high-pressure situations?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: If I ever encounter a deadline creep, my priority is to prioritize. This means I break down the deliverables into critical and non-critical items. I make sure to have proper communication with product owners and stakeholders to ensure that my changes are always visible. This lets them know what I am working on or if something is slipping because of the new requirements. I always maintain a good engineering standard and focus on incremental delivery to ensure quality is not compromised.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you explain a complex technical concept to a non-technical stakeholder?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I believe the best approach here is to look at things from their perspective. First, I put myself in the stakeholder's shoes and look at issues they encounter or expectations they have for the software. I address the technical requirements in terms of solutions that can be compared to real-world scenarios. This way, I avoid getting stuck in technical intricacies and concentrate on what aspects the stakeholder wants. Most importantly, I always do a reality check by asking them if I have captured their requirements correctly.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you keep your technical skills up to date?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: In my continuous learning journey, I always value doing over learning. This makes me stay on top of my game while also exposing me to new frameworks and tools. I like to keep my skills sharp by playing with new frameworks and reading blog posts from technical writers in companies that operate at scale. I also interact with other developers from the tech community through tech meetups to share knowledge. In my learning, I prefer practical applications of new frameworks and tools. If there is something interesting that I stumble upon, I always like to document and share my findings with the team.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you approach debugging a system or code you've never seen before?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: When debugging something I haven't seen before, my first step is to establish a baseline of the expected results. From there, I look at logs and system telemetry to establish the root of the failure. I use tools like git bisect to identify failure surfaces or reduce the number of variables in the system until I get something that behaves as expected. From then on, I follow through on the execution flow to find the source of the error, understand it from the git commits, and finally provide a fix and regression tests for the said failure.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to disagree with a team member?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: At one time, I was working on a project with another person where we had to decide between using a monolithic micro-framework or a decoupled modular design to address latency issues. We could not seem to agree on which path to take. The way I handled it is by suggesting we do a small proof of concept on both ends to compare failure surfaces and latency. This way, we could objectively analyze the technical debt and make an informed decision based on the technical merits of the project.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Do you have any questions for us?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: Yes, actually, I do have some questions. What would success look like for someone in the first 90 days in this position? How does the engineering team balance feature development and technical debt management in the company's current sprints?

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I am a computer engineering practitioner with a strong interest in developing robust and scalable systems and solving complex algorithmic problems. In my professional life, I have focused on software engineering, algorithms, and core architecture fundamentals. I enjoy being challenged technically and delivering high-quality software solutions from concept to high-level design. I am excited about this opportunity with your company because I believe it will contribute to my professional growth in delivering impactful solutions.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Why do you want to work for our company?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I have heard great things about working with your company, especially about the innovative approaches to the technical problems within our space. The company prides itself on technical excellence and empowers engineers to shape their careers. My core values resonate well with the company's ethos, and I want to bring my expertise in system analysis and reliable execution to contribute to the company's growth.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about a time you worked with a difficult team member.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I remember working with a team member who was quite reserved and did not seem to share the same level of enthusiasm for the project. When it came to collaborative deliverables, we had too many miscommunications which slowed down our deliveries. What I did was to request for a one-on-one meeting to understand how they preferred to communicate. With that understanding and task management tools, we were able to clearly define ownership and deliverables, removing all ambiguity from our collaborations.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you prioritize your tasks when handling multiple projects?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I always make a list of all tasks and categorize them based on their business priority, impact, and dependencies. I then identify the major deliverables and blockers to other activities and set them aside. To ensure I am giving each task my undivided attention, I time-block to guarantee a steady stream of focus. I also schedule regular check-ins with project managers to ensure that my priorities align with the changing organizational priorities.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Describe a project you are most proud of.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I am most proud of the systems project where I got to develop a software solution. I took full ownership of the project lifecycle from requirement gathering to implementation while making important decisions at each step of the way. The result was a software solution that optimized resource handling and algorithm efficiency which improved the overall performance by over 30% and simplified the maintenance process for the other engineers.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you handle receiving critical feedback?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: I welcome critical feedback as part of my growth journey as a software engineer. When delivering such feedback, I always request clarification first before actioning. Then, I break down the feedback to provide a practical step-by-step resolution. By following up with the feedback provider to show resolution progress, I show that I value their opinion and assume personal responsibility for my work.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology or domain quickly.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: Our team was faced with a challenging project that required us to adopt a new framework. None of us had any experience, but the project was time-sensitive and could not be canceled. I took it upon myself to quickly go through the documentation, set up a proof of concept, and identified patterns in the new framework. Within three days, I had fully integrated it into the project and provided a cheat sheet for the rest of the team to use as a guide.

trivial_interview_questions.question: How do you handle a situation where requirements change mid-project?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: When the requirements change during a project, my first focus is to determine the scope's impact, design implications, and effect on sprints. With this information, I present a list of options and trade-offs that can be considered. This helps the product owners make their decisions faster, and I can quickly adjust my project to incorporate the new requirements. Where possible, I do swift refactoring to keep the code clean to avoid technical debt.

trivial_interview_questions.question: Tell me about a time you took initiative without being asked.
trivial_interview_questions.answer: While working on our team's development sprints, I noticed that we spent too many hours on weekly testing and build processes without having a solid automation layer. I took it upon myself to create a lightweight script that could support us during the testing phase. It saved us hours of testing and building processes, allowing the team to redirect that time and energy towards actual feature development.

trivial_interview_questions.question: What motivates you in your day-to-day work?
trivial_interview_questions.answer: The thing that motivates me every day is working on hard problems and coming up with elegant technical solutions. It feels pretty awesome to write code that actually delivers business value and functions reliably. I am also motivated by working with smart people who challenge me to be even better at what I do.
